headline: How One Woman’s Quest for Clean Water Shook Up Trinidad, Texas

paragraphs.text: It started with a Facebook post in April that showed brown water pooling in a tub. What followed was the unraveling of Trinidad, Texas.

Jennifer Combs, 40, the woman who shared the post, was arrested in May as the city’s police chief claimed she was spreading false information about the water quality in Trinidad, a rural city about 70 miles southeast of Dallas.

After the charges against Ms. Combs were dropped, the police chief of the Trinidad Police Department resigned in June. Two city hall staffers resigned in July, forcing the mayor to hire interim help to run the city.

The turmoil in Trinidad reached a crescendo in September, when the state forced the city’s police department to disband after an investigation, leaving the community of about 800 residents without its own law enforcement.
“The total undoing of our city in the past few weeks since that happened has just been astonishing,” Dennis Haws, the mayor of Trinidad, said, referring to Ms. Combs’ arrest.

Trinidad hasn’t always been this turbulent. The city had long been quiet, anchored by its city hall building on a corner of Park Street by Texas State Highway 31. Down the street from the building, there is a gas station with wide lanes for tractor-trailers and a Dairy Queen, a staple of small towns in Texas.
Mr. Haws, who became mayor last year, moved to Trinidad about five years ago. He said that he has seen little crime since moving to the city.
“It’s just a pretty quiet place to live,” he said, “pretty typical small town Texas kind of feel.”

But there has been one long standing issue in Trinidad: the water. The city has an aging water plant, part of a broader infrastructure problem across Texas that results in billions of gallons of wasted water every year. In Trinidad, Mr. Haws said, the water pipes underground date back to the 1950s or 1960s and hasn’t been properly maintained.

State records dating back to 2003 show dozens of complaints about the water in Trinidad, including five made this year, according to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality. Those complaints have increased steadily since 2020.
“It’s just not been very well maintained,” Mr. Haws said about the water system. “It has been an ongoing situation.”
One complaint to the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality was filed on April 2, citing concerns from residents about faucets’ spouting brown water.

In early April, Ms. Combs posted an image on Facebook that showed a bathtub filled with brown water. Ms. Combs said a friend who lived in Trinidad shared the picture with her. Ms. Combs does not live in the city but nearby, and reports independently on the area for her website, TruthOutlaw.

“We are receiving reports of possible water quality issues, including concerns about bacteria and unsafe conditions,” the Facebook post said. “We understand not all Trinidad water appears this way. However, if yours does, please let us know. This is about public safety, transparency, and getting answers.”

The Trinidad Police Department pushed back on concerns about the water quality. In a statement shared on Facebook on April 6, the police department said that it was aware of concerns about the water, and that discoloration was possibly the result of rust or sediment that moved through water lines during maintenance. The statement also cautioned that false reports about public services could violate the Texas Penal Code.
About two weeks later, on April 21, the city of Trinidad instructed residents to boil their water for two minutes before drinking it.
Ms. Combs was arrested on May 8 for making a false report or alarm. She spent 23 hours in jail before being bailed out.
“It was very traumatizing,” Ms. Combs said to The New York Times. “I had never even had a speeding ticket before.”
Charles Gregory, the chief of the Trinidad Police Department at the time, addressed concerns about the water and the arrest of Ms. Combs in a Facebook post on May 10.

“It was a very cut-and-dry case,” Mr. Gregory wrote. “Some people believe I should stay quiet, but that’s not who I am. I did not take this position to be a ‘yes man.’ I took an oath to protect this city, to make it better, and that includes standing up for the truth when misinformation is being pushed.”
About two weeks after the arrest, a grand jury in Henderson County declined to indict Ms. Combs, and the case was dismissed.

What followed was a flurry of lawsuits, investigations and resignations. Mr. Gregory resigned from the police department in June without publicly saying why he was stepping down. Then the Texas Rangers, the state’s top investigative agency, started to look into the city's management. Soon after, the Trinidad city administrator and clerk resigned.
Ms. Combs filed a lawsuit in federal court in May against the city of Trinidad, Mr. Gregory and Cameron Beckham, who had also worked for the police department.
“I absolutely knew that I was falsely arrested and should not have been arrested,” Ms. Combs told The Times, adding that she felt that Mr. Gregory was “personally coming after” her.
Lawyers for Mr. Gregory and Mr. Beckham declined to comment on the case, citing the ongoing lawsuit.
“Mrs. Combs did not fabricate an emergency,” the lawsuit states. “She did not summon emergency responders. She did not trigger evacuations.”

The lawsuit, which seeks punitive damages, also names Marie Bannister, a Trinidad City Council member, as a defendant. The suit claims that Ms. Bannister was aware of water issues in Trinidad and worked to suppress reports from residents with concerns rather than address them. Ms. Bannister did not respond to a request for comment.

After an investigation into the Trinidad Police Department by the Texas Commission on Law Enforcement in August, the city of Trinidad was told in a letter on Sept. 9 that its police department “failed to meet minimum standards,” thus forcing it to disband its eight-member police force. A state inspection of the Police Department found that the agency could not prove it had at least one bulletproof vest per officer on duty, a proper evidence room and official policies on situations such as use of force and vehicle pursuit.

Mr. Haws has said he was not surprised to learn that the state’s investigation was forcing the city to disband the police department, citing issues in the past. Ms. Combs’s Facebook post about the brown water, Mr. Haws said, was not the only reason the state was investigating the department.
“There’s a 15-year history of an inability to properly maintain a police force,” he said. “But it certainly amplified everything and it put a spotlight on everything.”
At a City Council meeting the next week, Mr. Beckham, who was serving as the interim police chief at the time, said he wanted to keep his department active.
“But if the ship sinks, I’m going down with it. That’s all I have to say,” Mr. Beckham said before leaving the meeting.

Despite the turmoil in Trinidad, Mr. Haws said that some silver linings emerged. The city has contracted with an engineering firm to assess its water infrastructure. Mr. Haws also credited Ms. Combs in part for bringing greater awareness to the water issues in Trinidad, even if it resulted in her arrest.

“That’s the part that has been missed through all of this,” Mr. Haws said. “We’re a small city. We don’t have money laying around to do this with, and her goal was to hopefully put together enough information to go to the state of Texas.”

For now, the Henderson County Sheriff’s Office will help handle policing in Trinidad until the city can reach an agreement with other nearby police agencies. But the water concerns remain an issue. A section of the city was under a boil water notice for two months after Sept. 16. The city temporarily changed the disinfectant in its water system in late October, and residents have been advised that the taste or smell of the water could be different during the switch.
“The citizens, I think, by and large are tired of all of this,” Mr. Haws said. “They just want to live a peaceful life.”
